title: Volume 10 · Site Security and Hardening: Protecting the Company's Money
subtitle: Lessons 1–10: accounts, two-factor, least privilege, network exposure, keys and the first hour of an incident
outcomes: Close the account habits that make a site easy to enter, starting with the administrator
Specify two-factor authentication, session rules and network restrictions the host will enforce
Manage integration keys and the encryption key as assets with an owner and a rotation date
Run a security review a client can sign, and know what to do in the first hour of an incident

slides.kicker: Lesson 1 · Why it is your job
slides.title: The site holds the money, not just the data
bullets: A ledger with payment details and tax identifiers is a target, and the fastest route in is a shared login
The functional consultant does not administer servers, but does specify what must be enforced
Most incidents a consultant will meet are ordinary: a departed staff member, a shared password, a stale key
Security work is cheap when it is a checklist and expensive when it is an incident
Put it in the handover pack with a name and a review date, or it will not happen
slides.notes: Say plainly what is the host's job and what is the client's: the consultant specifies, the host enforces, the client owns the people. Without that sentence each party assumes the other has done the account review, and the departed warehouse manager still has a login.

slides.title: One person, one account, every time
bullets: Shared logins destroy the audit trail and make a departure impossible to unwind cleanly
The administrator account is for administration, not for daily invoicing
Every account has a real name, a role and a manager who confirms it is still needed
Departure procedure: disable on the last day, reassign open documents, and keep the record
Show the client the activity log once, because it answers the question they always ask later

rows: List every enabled user with role and manager
Confirm daily work is not done as administrator
Run a departure dry run with a test user

slides.notes: The departure dry run is what turns a policy into a capability. Most clients have never disabled an account while documents were open, and the first attempt is usually during a resignation, in a hurry. Rehearse it once with a test user.

slides.title: The single control that stops credential theft
bullets: Two-factor authentication is the highest-value control per minute of effort on any internet-facing site
Enforce it for roles that can see money, prices or personal data, and for every administrator
Check how recovery works before enforcing, or one lost phone becomes an outage
Enforce by role rather than asking politely, because optional security is decoration
Record who holds which device and who may reset it

rows: Confirm two-factor is available and enforced by role
Policy visible in the user form
Login now asks for a code
Extend to finance and sales roles
Register a second device for the owner
Test recovery with one device removed
Record device holders and reset authority

slides.notes: Enforce by role and rehearse the recovery before you switch it on for everyone. The worst outcome is a controller locked out at month end and no documented way back, which teaches the client that security costs them money.

slides.title: Give access like you are lending money
bullets: Least privilege means the smallest set of rights that lets the person finish today's work
Delete is the first right to withhold, because a deleted document is the hardest to reconstruct
Warehouse and company restrictions are part of privilege, not an afterthought, and they must be tested by logging in as the user
Role proliferation is a smell: fifty roles means nobody can describe who may do what
Review access quarterly against the org chart, and record every removal

rows: No role grants delete except one
Roles map to the org chart

slides.notes: Privilege is the area where a functional consultant has the most leverage and the least excuse, because the tools are all in the browser. The two-login test is the only proof that a restriction works. Run it, then write the access matrix down.

slides.title: Who can reach the login page at all
bullets: HTTPS everywhere is non-negotiable; a login form over plain HTTP is a password in a plain envelope
Restrict the administrative paths to known addresses where the host allows it, so the world only sees the login
Remote access for staff should be a VPN or a managed proxy, not an open port
Session timeouts belong to the risk appetite of the client, not to the default
Any restriction must be tested from outside, because 'should be blocked' is not a control
slides.notes: Most of this belongs to the host, and that is precisely why it must be written as a requirement with evidence. Ask for a screenshot of a refused connection from outside the network. A verbal assurance that it is locked down is not a control.

slides.title: Every key is a spare key to the ledger
bullets: API keys and e-Invoice credentials are privileges in disguise, so they need an owner, a scope and a review date
Never use one key for every integration, because revoking it then stops everything at once
Keys live in the host's secret store or the site configuration, never in a spreadsheet or a chat message
Rotate on a schedule and immediately when someone with access leaves
Log which integration uses which key, or revocation becomes guesswork

rows: Inventory every integration and its credential
Record owner and purpose per key
Test revocation on one spare key

slides.notes: The revocation test is worth the ten minutes: revoke a spare key and confirm only its integration stops. Clients discover during an incident that one key serves four systems, and then they cannot cut off the compromised one without stopping trading.

slides.title: The one file that cannot be regenerated
bullets: The site encryption key protects stored credentials and encrypted fields, and losing it damages the site permanently
Store it outside the backup, with two named holders and a documented retrieval path
Rotate it only with a plan, because rotation has to re-encrypt what it protects
Test retrieval: the holder should be able to produce it without the consultant's help
Record the key's location in the handover pack as a pointer, never the key itself

rows: No key material in the document

slides.notes: This is the item clients nod at and then fail. Test retrieval with the actual holder in the room, and watch where they go, because if the answer is 'ask the consultant' the plan is not finished. Never put the key itself in the handover pack.

slides.title: The logs nobody reads until it is too late
bullets: Failed logins, permission changes and document deletions are the three signals worth watching
Activity history per document answers the practical question: who changed this, and when
Alerts should reach a person, not a folder; a weekly summary is enough for a small site
An audit trail nobody can query is a story, not a control
Agree the retention period with the client's auditor before the first incident
slides.notes: Keep the watching small enough to survive: three signals, one weekly summary, one named recipient. A client who is asked to read a security dashboard will not, but a client who receives four lines on a Monday will.

slides.title: One page a client can sign
bullets: A security review is a checklist with evidence, not an opinion, and it fits on one page
Each line: the control, the evidence, the date and who confirmed it
Include the items you cannot verify yourself, marked as host-confirmed with a date
Repeat it quarterly and after every departure, because both change the answer
The signed page is what protects the client and the consultant when something goes wrong
slides.notes: One page, dated, signed. That document is the difference between a professional engagement and an argument after an incident. It also makes the next review fast, because you compare against the last signed page.

slides.title: If it happens, the sequence matters
bullets: Contain first: disable the account, revoke the key, and do not stop to diagnose
Preserve evidence before cleaning: export the logs you will need and note the times
Tell the client's owner in one message with facts, not a narrative of discovery
Restore and verify using the drill from the continuity chapter, then re-enter the window
Write the incident note within a day, and change one control as a result

rows: Disable the affected account and revoke its keys
Export logs and record times before any cleanup
Notify the client owner with the facts
Restore the last good backup if data was altered
Site returns to the known state
Write the incident note and change one control

slides.notes: The order is contain, preserve, notify, restore, verify, learn. Consultants who start by investigating burn the hour that mattered. Rehearse the disabling step in a test account so the first time is not during an incident.

lab.title: Lab · Harden the Seri Murni site and sign the review
steps: Export the enabled user list, identify shared logins and write the departure procedure
Disable a test user who holds an open document and reassign the document to their manager
Enforce two-factor for administrators and finance, enrol a second device and test recovery
Test one warehouse restriction with two logins and attach both screenshots to the review
Confirm HTTPS, session timeout and restricted administrative paths, with host evidence dated
Inventory every integration key with its owner, then revoke a spare key and prove only that integration stops
Locate the encryption key through its holder without your help, and record the pointer in the handover pack
Complete the one-page security review, sign it, and rehearse the first three steps of the incident sequence
lab.done: A signed one-page security review with dated evidence, no shared accounts, two-factor enforced by role, keys inventoried with an owner, and a holder who produced the encryption key unaided.

quiz.question: Why is two-factor authentication the highest-value control on an internet-facing site?
options: It encrypts the database
It stops a stolen or guessed password from being enough on its own
It replaces role permissions
It reduces hosting cost
quiz.why: Most real incidents begin with credentials. Two-factor makes the stolen password insufficient, which is a large risk reduction for a few minutes of configuration per user.

quiz.question: What makes a departure procedure a capability rather than a policy?
options: A signature from management
A dry run with a test user who holds open documents
A paragraph in the handover pack
An annual reminder
quiz.why: The hard part is reassigning open documents while disabling access. Until someone has done it once under no pressure, the policy has never been tested.

quiz.question: Why must an integration key belong to exactly one integration?
options: Because keys expire quickly
Because otherwise revoking a compromised key stops several integrations at once
Because the system limits key count
Because each key needs its own password
quiz.why: Revocation is the containment step in an incident. A shared key turns a surgical response into an outage that stops trading.

quiz.question: What is the correct answer if nobody can produce the encryption key without the consultant?
options: It is fine because the backup exists
The plan is unfinished and retrieval must be drilled with the named holder
The key can be regenerated
The host will supply a new one
quiz.why: The key cannot be regenerated without losing what it protects, and the backup usually does not contain it. Until two named holders can retrieve it unaided, there is no plan.

quiz.question: What is the right first move in the first hour of a suspected compromise?
options: Investigate the cause
Contain access, then preserve the evidence before cleaning anything
Restore from last night's backup immediately
Email the whole company
quiz.why: Containment stops the damage; preserving the logs keeps the cause findable. Restoring first, or investigating first, destroys the evidence you need for both decisions.

memory.spine: One person one account, two factors, the smallest privilege, the fewest open doors, and every key with an owner and a date.

device.label: Least privilege, then prove it
expansion: Nobody shares a login, and the administrator account is not a workspace
Two-factor is enforced by role before anything else is discussed
Privilege is the smallest set that finishes today's work, tested by logging in as the user
Network and keys are restrictions with evidence, not assurances
The one-page review is dated and signed, and the encryption key has two named holders

cards.q: Why is a shared login worse than a weak password?
cards.a: Because it destroys the audit trail and makes a departure impossible to unwind. You cannot disable one person without disabling everyone.

cards.q: What evidence proves a restriction actually restricts?
cards.a: A second login that shows the difference, or a refused connection from outside the network. Configuration alone is not evidence.

cards.q: What must exist before two-factor is enforced for finance?
cards.a: A tested recovery path and a second enrolled device, plus a recorded reset authority, so month end cannot be lost to a phone.

cards.q: How should integration keys and e-Invoice credentials be managed?
cards.a: One key per integration, an owner and purpose in a register, storage outside documents, a rotation date, and a tested revocation.

cards.q: What are the first two moves in a suspected compromise?
cards.a: Contain access — disable the account, revoke the key — then preserve the logs before anything is cleaned or restored.

trap.what: The client says the host handles security, so no account review is done and the encryption key lives only in the consultant's notes.
trap.why: The host protects the server; it cannot stop a shared login or a stale key. Write the split of responsibility, run the review quarterly, and drill key retrieval with two named holders.

narration: This chapter exists because the site holds the money, and the easiest way in is not technical. Start with accounts: one person one login, no shared warehouse account, and the administrator kept for administration rather than daily invoicing. Write the departure procedure and rehearse it with a test user who holds open documents, because that is the step clients fail under pressure. Then enforce two factor by role, beginning with administrators and finance, after proving that recovery works, so a lost phone is not a lost month end. Privilege is next: withhold delete, restrict by warehouse, and prove it with a second login rather than a configuration screenshot. Network exposure and keys belong to the host and to you jointly, so ask for evidence of a refused connection from outside, keep one key per integration with an owner and a rotation date, and test revocation. Find the encryption key through its named holder without your help. Then sign the one page review, dated, with the items you cannot verify marked as host confirmed. And if something happens, contain access first, preserve the logs second, notify the owner third, and only then restore and verify.
